def: Drugs that constrict blood vessels to raise blood pressure, used in shock when fluids fail. Examples include norepinephrine, vasopressin and phenylephrine.
Activation of a receptor by a drug or ligand, producing a biological response. An agonist mimics the natural signal.
Variation in red blood cell size on a blood smear, reflected by a high red cell distribution width (RDW). Seen in iron deficiency and other anemias.
Located in front of the vertebral column. Prevertebral sympathetic ganglia (celiac, superior and inferior mesenteric) supply abdominal organs.
Formation of the lipid-rich myelin sheath around axons, by oligodendrocytes in the CNS and Schwann cells in the periphery. Greatly speeds nerve conduction.
Relating to the coccyx, the tailbone at the end of the spine. The single coccygeal spinal nerve is the 31st pair.
A tongue muscle that retracts the tongue and pulls it up and back. Innervated by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII).
A tongue muscle that depresses and retracts the tongue. Innervated by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII).
Derived from many different cell clones. Reactive lymphoid proliferation is polyclonal, whereas lymphomas are monoclonal.
Having features of both lymphocytes and plasma cells, as in lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma (Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia), which makes IgM.
A map of the body laid over the primary motor or sensory cortex, with the face and hands drawn disproportionately large because they have the densest innervation.
Loss of normal restraint on behavior, producing impulsive, socially inappropriate acts. Characteristic of frontal lobe damage.
Through the skull. Transcranial Doppler ultrasound measures blood flow velocity in brain arteries, for example to detect vasospasm.
A point on the right lower abdomen, about one-third of the way from the anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus. Tenderness here suggests appendicitis.
Growing as a mass that projects into a lumen, like a polyp. Applies to some colon tumors.
Presence of gas within the wall of an organ, as in pneumatosis intestinalis seen in necrotizing enterocolitis.
Staining darker than normal because of dense, abnormal nuclear chromatin. A feature of malignant cells.
Without growth of new blood vessels. Nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy shows microaneurysms, hemorrhages and hard exudates.
A nonbenzodiazepine hypnotic ("Z-drug") that acts on the GABA-A receptor to treat insomnia. Very short half-life.
An orexin receptor antagonist that promotes sleep, used for insomnia.
An inflated sense of self-importance or abilities, seen in mania.
By a route other than the digestive tract, typically injection (intravenous, intramuscular or subcutaneous).
Developing from a single fertilized egg that splits in two, giving identical twins with the same genetic makeup.
A peritoneal fold between the liver and the lesser curvature of the stomach, forming the front of the lesser sac. Part of the lesser omentum; carries the left gastric vessels.
A peritoneal fold connecting the greater curvature of the stomach to the spleen. Carries the short gastric arteries.
Relating to osteoclasts, the cells that break down bone. The first phase of Paget disease of bone is osteoclastic.

Splitting light into two rays, so crystals appear bright and change color under polarized light. Monosodium urate crystals (gout) are negatively birefringent; calcium pyrophosphate (pseudogout) positively.
Plugs of keratin and oil in hair follicles. Open comedones are blackheads and closed comedones are whiteheads, the primary lesions of acne.
Having a central dimple. Molluscum contagiosum papules are umbilicated.
A direct thrombin inhibitor given intravenously, used to treat heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. Cleared by the liver.
A nonrandom group of congenital defects: vertebral anomalies, anal atresia, cardiac defects, tracheoesophageal fistula, renal anomalies and limb defects.
A penicillin with extended spectrum, including ampicillin and amoxicillin, active against some gram-negative rods and Enterococcus. Destroyed by beta-lactamases unless combined with an inhibitor.
Streptococcus pneumoniae, an encapsulated gram-positive diplococcus and leading cause of pneumonia, meningitis and otitis media.
Located in front of the kneecap. Prepatellar bursitis ("housemaid's knee") is usually from Staphylococcus aureus after kneeling.
Failure of a fractured bone to heal. High-risk sites include the proximal fifth metatarsal and scaphoid.
Relating to seminoma, a germ cell tumor of the testis made of uniform cells with clear cytoplasm. Typically has normal AFP and radiosensitivity.
Reduced movement. In the heart, decreased contraction of a wall segment; in neurology, reduced spontaneous movement as in parkinsonism.
Rotation of the forearm so the palm faces down (or backward). In nursemaid elbow, the child's forearm is held pronated.
A hip flexor muscle in the iliac fossa that joins the psoas major to form the iliopsoas. Innervated by the femoral nerve.
A form of lipopolysaccharide lacking the O antigen, found in Neisseria and Haemophilus. Acts as an endotoxin and varies antigenically.
A second surface molecule needed with the main receptor for entry or signaling. HIV uses CD4 plus CCR5 or CXCR4.
Inflammation at the site where tendons or ligaments insert into bone. Characteristic of spondyloarthropathies such as reactive arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis.
Viral infection of the larynx, trachea and bronchi, known as croup. Causes barking cough and inspiratory stridor; usually parainfluenza.
Located inside red blood cells, as with malaria and Babesia.
The pigment that malaria parasites make by polymerizing toxic heme released from digested hemoglobin. Blocking its formation is how chloroquine works.
A parasitic flatworm (fluke), such as Schistosoma and liver flukes. They have complex life cycles with a snail host.
Non-enveloped, double-stranded segmented RNA viruses. Rotavirus, the leading cause of pediatric diarrhea, is a member.
A bony outgrowth that serves as a tendon attachment site, with its own growth center. Osgood-Schlatter disease involves the tibial tuberosity apophysis.
Untwisting of a twisted structure, such as manual or surgical untwisting of a torsed testis or ovary to restore blood flow.
Having never given birth to a viable infant.
Located outside the peritoneal cavity, either retroperitoneal or subperitoneal. The bladder is mostly extraperitoneal.
Describing glands that release secretions by exocytosis without losing cell material, such as salivary and eccrine sweat glands.
Failure of the body's compensatory mechanisms, producing clinical deterioration, such as acute worsening of heart failure or cirrhosis.
An x-ray of the uterus and fallopian tubes using injected contrast, mainly to check tubal patency in infertility.
A contrast imaging study of the bladder and urethra. Voiding cystourethrography detects vesicoureteral reflux and urethral valves.
Present without symptoms or obvious signs, detected only by testing. Subclinical hypothyroidism has high TSH with normal free T4.
A selective and differential culture medium for gram-negative bacteria. Lactose fermenters (E. coli, Klebsiella) form pink colonies; nonfermenters stay colorless.
A paper pH test used to detect ruptured membranes: amniotic fluid is alkaline and turns the paper blue, while vaginal fluid is acidic.
Treatment combining chemotherapy and radiation therapy at the same time, to make tumors more sensitive to radiation.
To add a phosphate group to a molecule, usually a protein, switching its activity on or off. Done by kinases.
A steroid intermediate in cortisol synthesis made from progesterone by 17-alpha-hydroxylase. Markedly elevated in 21-hydroxylase deficiency (congenital adrenal hyperplasia).
A class of oral diabetes drugs (glipizide, glyburide, glimepiride) that close pancreatic beta cell potassium channels to release insulin. Can cause hypoglycemia and weight gain.
Having an ester bond, typically a fatty acid attached to cholesterol or glycerol. Cholesterol is stored in esterified form.
To make the inside of a cell less negative, moving membrane potential toward threshold. Opening sodium or calcium channels causes depolarization.
Swelling that does not leave a dent when pressed, as in myxedema of hypothyroidism and lymphedema.
Radioactive iodine (I-131) taken up by the thyroid, used to treat hyperthyroidism and thyroid cancer, or to image the gland.
Through the sphenoid sinus. The transsphenoidal approach through the nose is the usual route for removing pituitary adenomas.
General body build or physique. Marfanoid habitus describes tall stature with long limbs.
Resembling Marfan syndrome with tall stature, long thin limbs and fingers. Seen in MEN 2B and homocystinuria.
The synthesis of glycogen from glucose, stimulated by insulin in liver and muscle via glycogen synthase.
An alpha-glucosidase inhibitor that slows intestinal carbohydrate digestion, lowering post-meal glucose. Side effects are flatulence and diarrhea.
According to genetic makeup, as opposed to physical appearance. For example, a genotypically XY person with androgen insensitivity may look female.
